title: How the brain turns up the thermostat in a fever
examples: How does the body make a fever?
Why do you feel cold when you have a fever?
Why do you sweat when a fever breaks?

explain.say: A fever is not the body overheating by accident. It is the brain deliberately turning up its thermostat while the immune system fights an infection.

draw.text: How the brain turns up the thermostat in a fever

explain.say: When immune cells detect germs, they release chemical messengers that travel to the hypothalamus. These raise its set point, the temperature it aims for, by a degree or two.
Now your normal temperature counts as too cold, so you feel chilly. You shiver, and skin blood vessels narrow to keep heat in, until your temperature climbs to the new set point and holds there.
When the infection is under control, the messengers fade and the set point drops back. Now you are too warm for it, so you sweat and flush until you cool down: the fever breaks.

faq.q: What makes the body's thermostat go up?
faq.a: Immune cells fighting an infection release chemical messengers, called pyrogens. In the hypothalamus they trigger a substance called prostaglandin E2, which raises the temperature set point.
asks: Tell me about germs being detected

faq.q: Why do you feel cold at the start of a fever?
faq.a: The brain has raised its target temperature, so your actual temperature is now below the target. The body responds as if it were cold: you feel chilly, shiver and want blankets, which heats you up.
asks: Tell me about chills and shivers
Why do I shiver with a fever?

faq.q: Why do you sweat when a fever breaks?
faq.a: When the set point returns to normal, your body is warmer than the new target, so it sweats and widens skin blood vessels to lose the extra heat.
asks: Tell me about sweating as it breaks

faq.q: Why does the body make a fever?
faq.a: Scientists think a higher temperature helps the immune system: some germs grow less well, and some immune cells work faster when slightly warmer.
asks: Is fever part of fighting germs?

faq.a: The hypothalamus, a small area at the base of the brain, acts as the body's thermostat. It compares your temperature with its set point and triggers shivering or sweating to correct it.

facts: Normal body temperature is around 37 degrees Celsius, varying a little through the day.
Prostaglandin E2 acting in the hypothalamus raises the temperature set point during fever.

quiz.say: Why do people shiver at the start of a fever?
quiz.show: Why do people shiver at the start of a fever?

options.show: The brain's set point has gone up, so the body heats itself
options.say: The brain's set point has gone up, so the body heats itself

quiz.why: With a higher target temperature, the body treats its current temperature as too cold and shivers to warm up.

wrong.0: It happens whatever the room temperature; the change is in the brain's target.
wrong.2: The shivering is the brain's response, not germs acting on muscles.
